papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc resource-library lesson page that explains the quantum Zeno effect conceptually and says how it lets photons interact.

assertions.value: The authors state that the page explains the Zeno effect at a conceptual level and does not give the full mathematics, and they point to a separate article for the rigorous mathematics.
quotes: the point of this page is to explain on a more conceptual level, without giving the full mathematics.
While very good work has been done to work out the rigorous mathematics behind this effect
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states its own scope in the opening paragraph.
assertions.reader_inference: The page reports no experiment or measurement of its own; it is an explainer, so its claims rest on cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that components of a computer need to interact for it to compute, that this is fairly easy with electricity but surprisingly hard with photons, and that the Quantum Zeno Effect enables that interaction.
quotes: the components within the computer need to be able to interact with each other.
This is fairly easy with electricity, but surprisingly hard with photons.
Fortunately, the Quantum Zeno Effect enables that interaction.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's framing of its own technology; no evidence is given on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum systems are affected by observation, and that a system can therefore be stopped by observing it.
quotes: Quantum mechanically, the situation is different because systems are affected by observing them
In other words, a system can be stopped by observing it.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof on the page; the page's own derivation is a scaling sketch.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the standard quantum Zeno effect; the page's wording is informal.

assertions.value: The authors state that various experiments have shown the effect to be real, including experiments by members of their team. The page names no experiment, setup or result.
quotes: Various experiments have been performed to show that this is a very real effect, including by members of our team
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited, unspecified result; the linked work is not in the page text.

assertions.value: The authors define 'observing' loosely as strongly interacting with something else, and state that no human or other sentient being needs to be aware of the result.
quotes: it just means strongly interacting with something else and it doesn't need a human or other sentient being to be aware of the result.
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines its own use of the word 'observing' in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that a classical system can be measured without any effect on it, so a watched arrow moves exactly like an unwatched arrow, and that the arrow paradox is resolved mathematically by calculus.
assertions.anchor: How does it work?, page text
quotes: a classical system can be measured without having any effect on it; a watched arrow moves exactly like an unwatched arrow.
it takes calculus to resolve the arrow paradox
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the name comes from Zeno's arrow paradox, developed by Zeno of Elea between 500 and 400 BCE.
assertions.anchor: How does it work?, page text
quotes: developed by the ancient Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea between 500 and 400 BCE.
assertions.certainty_reason: A historical attribution given without a source on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that, quantum mechanically, any measurement apparatus changes the system it measures, and that this is known as projective measurement, which projects a state into the result of the measurement.
assertions.anchor: How does it work?, page text
quotes: No matter how good a measurement apparatus is, it fundamentally does change the system it measures
This is known as projective measurement ; it projects a state into the result of the measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum mechanics is based on the movement of probability amplitude, which is proportional to the square root of probability, and that measuring before much amplitude builds up gives a very small squared amplitude, so many quick measurements can stop the system from moving entirely.
assertions.anchor: How does it work?, page text
quotes: Quantum mechanics is based on the movement of probability amplitude, which is proportional to the square root of probability.
If we measure before much amplitude can build up then the amplitude squared is going to be very small
Making a lot of quantum measurements quickly therefore can stop the system from moving entirely.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conceptual argument without a full derivation.

assertions.value: For a system that would normally transition between two states, the authors state that with N evenly spaced measurements the amplitude that builds up in each period is proportional to 1/N, so the probability of state 1 in each period is proportional to 1/N squared, and the overall probability of ever finding the system in state 1 is proportional to N/N squared, which is 1/N, and goes to zero as the number of measurements becomes large.
assertions.anchor: How does it work?, equations paragraph, page text
quotes: If we measure it N N N (evenly spaced) times then the amplitude a 2 a^2 a 2 which can build up during each time period is proportional to 1 / N 1/N 1/ N
making the probability to measure in state 1 1 1 ( P 1 = ∣ a 1 ∣ 2 P_1=|a_1|^2 P 1 = ∣ a 1 ∣ 2 ) proportional to 1 / N 2 1/N^2 1/ N 2 .
this will be proportional to N / N 2 = 1 / N N/N^2=1/N N / N 2 = 1/ N and therefore will go to zero as the number of measurements becomes large.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proportionality sketch on a lesson page; the page says it gives only a minimal amount of equations and no full mathematics. It is not a stated theorem with conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the amplitude as 'a 2' where the page's own next clause refers to a_1; this looks like a typo for a_1. The argument assumes the amplitude per period scales with the period length and that the periods are short.

assertions.value: The authors state that the argument needs both the fact that quantum measurements change the system and the fact that the important quantity in quantum mechanics is amplitude, not probability.
assertions.anchor: How does it work?, end of equations paragraph, page text
quotes: Note that this needed both the fact that quantum measurements change the system and the fact that the important quantity in quantum mechanics is amplitude, not probability, to work correctly.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about their own sketch; not proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using some of their nonlinear optics systems, they can engineer a situation where a single light particle effectively watches another light particle, which gives light particles interactions with each other.
assertions.anchor: But how is this useful?, page text
quotes: using some of our nonlinear optics systems, we can engineer a situation where a single light particle can effectively watch another light particle.
In this way, we can make light particles, which are famously hard to make interact , have interactions with each other.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own systems; the page gives no device, data or reference for it.

assertions.value: The authors state that light particles move naturally, which makes information transfer relatively simple, and do not interact much with noise sources because they are not charged, but that light has traditionally been weak because its particles are hard to make interact with each other.
assertions.anchor: But how is this useful?, page text
quotes: light particles naturally move, making information transfer relatively simple, and since light particles aren't charged they don't interact much with noise sources.
the weakness of light has traditionally been that it is hard to make the light particles interact with each other.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement without evidence on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that a particle is stopped from moving from one component on a chip to another only if a different particle is already there, and that this can be used to build a quantum computer by providing an entangling gate between light particles.
assertions.anchor: But how is this useful?, page text
quotes: we only stop a particle from moving from one component on a chip to another if a different particle is already there, and this can be used to build a quantum computer by providing an entangling gate between light particles.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes how its approach yields an entangling gate; no gate data or fidelity is given on the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page gives no gate fidelity, success rate or device result.

assertions.value: The authors state that Zeno effects are useful in many other ways, for example guiding a system into different states when the measurement changes it slightly each time, and they defer this to a different discussion.
assertions.anchor: But how is this useful?, last paragraph, page text
quotes: Zeno effects are useful in many other ways too.
this is a subject for a different discussion.
